newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan analysts see no major rupee depreciation.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan analysts see no major rupee depreciation.

text.p: The Pakistani rupee is likely to gain against the dollar in the next few days after Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz ruled out any early exchange rate change, dealers and analysts said on Saturday.
"I do not see any need for an exchange rate adjustment at the moment," Aziz told Reuters Financial Television on Friday ahead of his budget speech for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June).
The rupee opened steady on Saturday at 41.82 to the dollar in the kerb market, but dealers said it was set to rise.
The State (central) Bank of Pakistan rate, last changed on May 23, was 40.3900/40.5900 against the dollar.
"With no talk of a devaluation in the budget, the rupee is likely to remain strong till the next depreciation," kerb dealer Owais Kalia of Khanani & Kalia International said.
He said the rupee could rise to 41.50 against the dollar in the next few days as speculators who had held back dollars on hopes of a post-budget devaluation unloaded their holdings.

After keeping its official rate steady for six months, the central bank has moved the rupee lower three times since April 23, prompting kerb players to speculate on a further adjustment before the end of the fiscal year on June 30.
Bankers say the rupee's real effective exchange rate had appreciated 9.3 percent between October and March while the nominal effective exchange rate had soared 3.9 percent.
The SBP has depreciated the rupee by 0.67 percent since April 23 and analysts say the local currency is still overvalued by about five percent on a real trade-weighted basis.

The chief economist at a foreign bank said the kerb market premium over the official rate could bounce back to four or five percent as the central bank was likely to follow a crawling peg depreciation policy to keep the rupee competitive.
"But I do not foresee a large devaluation till September," said the economist, who asked not to be named.
He said the exportable surplus between July and September is usually low. "Any deep cut in the rupee value before September will only add to the current account deficit," he said.
Aziz said the previous government led by Benazir Bhutto had devalued the rupee by 30 percent against the dollar during its three-year term, but failed to stimulate exports.

"Devaluation also leads to higher cost of imported goods and therefore to inflation," he said. "If we succeed in stabilising our inflation and our budget deficit, then we can maintain a more stable exchange rate in line with the world currencies."
The economist said the government was banking on improved productivity and lower inflationary pressure by the end of the year which would improve competitiveness and the trade account.
However, he said the central bank should speed up its small adjustments as any devaluation pressure in September-November would make foreign debt servicing a tough task.
"An estimated $1.6 billion of repayments are due in this period," he said. Devaluation would make debt servicing, already equal to 70 percent of tax revenue, more costly, he added.
